LESSON OBJECTIVE

Evaluate composite functions by reading two graphs in the correct order.

f(g(x)) means read g(x) first, then use that result as the input on graph f.
CORE IDEA
A function transforms an input into an output. A composite function chains two transformations. The first output becomes the second input; changing the order can change the answer.
KEY DEFINITIONS
Composition: f∘g(x)=f(g(x)). Inner function: evaluated first. Outer function: evaluated second. Domain: inputs for which a function is defined.
CORE RULE
For f(g(a)), read the y-value at x=a on graph g, call it b, then read the y-value at x=b on graph f. For g(f(a)), reverse the graph order. Both inputs must be in their respective domains.
HOW IT WORKS

1. Identify the inner function.
  2. Find its output on the first graph.
  3. Use that output as the input on the second graph.
  4. Read the final output.
  5. For restricted graphs, verify both steps exist.
WORKED EXAMPLES

Example 1 — Graph A

f(g(1)): g(1)=2(1)−1=1; f(1)=1+2=3. So f(g(1))=3.

Example 2 — Reverse order

g(f(1)): f(1)=3; g(3)=2(3)−1=5. Reversing the order changes 3 to 5.

Example 3 — Absolute value

Graph B: g(−1)=4, then f(4)=|4|=4. So f(g(−1))=4.

Example 4 — Curved graph

Graph C: g(2)=−2, then f(−2)=(−2)²−1=3.

Example 5 — Domain restriction

Graph D: g(x)=2−x on [0,4], f(x)=x+1 on [−2,1]. To form f(g(x)), require −2≤2−x≤1. Thus 1≤x≤4. For example, f(g(1))=f(1)=2.

COMMON MISTAKES

• Reading the outer graph first.
  • Stopping after the inner output.
  • Assuming f(g(x))=g(f(x)).
  • Using an output outside the outer function’s domain.
  • Confusing the viewing window with a restricted domain.
EXAM STRATEGY
Draw two arrows: input → inner graph output → outer graph output. When endpoints are restricted, verify the intermediate output belongs to the second graph before reporting a value.
QUICK CHECK
Graph A: f(g(0))=1. Graph B: g(f(−2))=1. Graph D: g(f(−2)) is undefined because f(−2)=−1 is outside g’s domain [0,4].
LESSON RECAP
Inside first, outside second. Use each graph’s y-value as the next graph’s x-value. Composition order and domain restrictions matter.
